ogDesc: Camp on Pha Chana Dai for Thailand's first sunrise over the Mekong, then come down for Pha Taem, Sao Chaliang and the two-colour river. With shuttle times, fees and the real season to go.
h1:
Catch Thailand's First Light at Pha Chana Dai,
Then See Pha Taem in One Trip
intro: Pha Chana Dai is the spot the Thai Meteorological Department uses as the reference point for where the sun rises first in the whole country. It sits at the far eastern edge of the Dong Na Tham forest, inside Pha Taem National Park in Khong Chiam district, and only officially reopened on 1 June 2025 after a long closure. The way that really works is to camp on the cliff for one night, wake up for first light over the Mekong and the mountains on the Lao side, then come back down to take in Pha Taem, Sao Chaliang and the two-colour river the same day. This 2-day, 1-night plan lines the shuttle times, entrance fees and timing up with how it actually runs on the ground, and tells you straight where it gets rough.

blocks.html: First thing to understand: Pha Chana Dai is not a drive-up-and-photograph-it spot. The viewpoint itself sits deep in the Dong Na Tham forest, and ordinary cars can't get up there. You park at the Dong Na Tham checkpoint and switch to a local vehicle (a pickup or one of the park's tour trucks) to go the rest of the way, on fixed up-and-down shuttle times. For sunrise, the sensible move is to spend a night on the cliff, because the morning run leaves as early as 4:30 a.m. and by the time you reach the viewpoint the sky is just starting to lighten.

blocks.text: What and where is Pha Chana Dai, and why go

blocks.html: Pha Chana Dai is a sandstone cliff on the bank of the Mekong, in the Dong Na Tham forest of Pha Taem National Park, in Na Pho Klang sub-district, Khong Chiam. What makes it special is that it's the coordinate where you see the sun come up before anywhere else in Thailand, looking across the Mekong to the mountains on the Lao PDR side. In the late-rains, early-cool window you've got a chance at a sea of mist drifting over the river. There's a natural stand of two-needle pines on the cliff and a camping ground for an overnight stay. The site used to open in stretches and then close again; it only came back fully on 1 June 2025, so it's still a corner most people haven't gotten around to.

items: Park entrance fee — Thai adults 40 THB, children 20 THB · foreign adults 400 THB, children 200 THB
Camping fee — 30 THB per person · no tent of your own? The park rents them for around 225 THB each (with a sleeping mat and pillow)
Getting up the cliff — cars can't make it; park at the Dong Na Tham checkpoint and switch to a local vehicle, on fixed up-and-down shuttle times
Viewpoint vs. camping ground — about 800 m apart and walkable; it's a short morning walk out to catch the light
Facilities — separate men's and women's toilets, but no electricity, so bring a flashlight/power bank and your own food. Mobile signal is True and AIS

blocks.title: Pha Chana Dai up-and-down shuttle times
blocks.html: There are 3 runs up from the Dong Na Tham checkpoint — morning 04:30–06:30 · midday 10:30–13:00 · evening 16:00–18:00. The runs down are 07:30–09:30 · 14:00–15:00 · 19:00–19:30. If you want sunrise without camping, take the evening run up to sleep over and walk out to the viewpoint before dawn. Always check the latest times with the park before you go, as they shift with the season. Call 045-252-541.

blocks.text: Day 1 — into Khong Chiam, take in Pha Taem, then up to sleep on the cliff

blocks.html: Ubon city to Khong Chiam is about 80 km, an hour and a half of driving. On day one we knock out the lower sights first — Pha Taem and Sao Chaliang, which sit right by the access road and are easy to get to. Then in the afternoon we head to the Dong Na Tham checkpoint to catch the evening shuttle up Pha Chana Dai, arriving in time to pitch the tent before dark and catch sunset from the cliff too.

blocks.label: Day 1
blocks.title: Ubon city → Pha Taem → Sao Chaliang → Dong Na Tham checkpoint → camp on Pha Chana Dai

items.activity: Leave Ubon city heading for Khong Chiam district. Stop to fill up the tank, grab water and snacks, and pack dinner and breakfast to take along.
items.note: Around 80 km, about 1.5 hours · there are no shops on Pha Chana Dai, so bring every meal yourself

items.activity: Enter Pha Taem National Park to see the prehistoric rock paintings, roughly 3,000–4,000 years old, on the cliff face above the Mekong. Take the path down to view the art, then loop up to the viewpoint.
items.note: Open 06:00–16:30 · Thai adult entry 40 THB, children 20 THB · the way down is stone steps, so sneakers are comfier · keep your ticket in case you use it again at other spots in the park

items.activity: Stop at Sao Chaliang, the mushroom-shaped stone pillars carved by wind and water over millions of years, just a little before the park headquarters. They photograph well at any time of day.
items.note: Same park area, no extra entry fee · the midday sun is strong, so bring a hat and an umbrella

items.activity: Head down for lunch in Khong Chiam town. Pick a riverside spot that cooks with Mekong fish — think tom yum with giant catfish, grilled fish or fish larb.
items.note: Fresh Mekong fish is the local specialty here; price goes by the size of the fish, and ordering dishes to share works out better value · this is your last proper, filling meal before heading up the cliff

items.activity: Arrive at the Dong Na Tham checkpoint, park up, pay the entrance and camping fees, then catch the local vehicle up Pha Chana Dai on the evening run (16:00–18:00).
items.note: Cars can't get up; you switch to a park/local vehicle · ask the fare at the checkpoint, charged by number of people/vehicle · leave time to make the run

items.activity: Reach the Pha Chana Dai camping ground, pitch your tent and get sorted before dark, then walk out to the cliff-edge viewpoint to catch the cool breeze and watch the sun set behind the Lao mountains.
items.note: The camping ground is about 800 m from the viewpoint · no electricity, so bring a flashlight and power bank · the wind is strong and it gets cold at night, so pack a warm layer even in the hot season

items.activity: Eat the dinner you packed, sit out and stargaze on the cliff — on a clear night you'll see the Milky Way plainly. Turn in early, since tomorrow you're up before 5 a.m.
items.note: Carry every bit of trash back down with you · set an alarm for around 4:30 a.m. to leave time to walk to the viewpoint before first light

blocks.title: Want first light without an overnight stay
blocks.html: If you really don't want to camp, you can take the 04:30 morning run from the Dong Na Tham checkpoint — but that means getting up in the middle of the night from your lodging in Khong Chiam and driving over in time to make the shuttle, which puts a lot of pressure on the clock. We think one night in a tent on the cliff is the easier call and gets you far more of the atmosphere.

blocks.text: Day 2 — Thailand's first light, then down for the two-colour river

blocks.html: This morning is the highlight of the trip. Up before 5 a.m., walk to the cliff-edge viewpoint and wait for first light to slowly push the horizon up on the Lao side. If you're lucky in the late-rains, early-cool season, there'll be a sea of mist drifting over the Mekong too. Once you've got your fill of photos, take the morning run down and come back to take in the two-colour river and a bite to eat in Khong Chiam before driving home.

blocks.label: Day 2
blocks.title: First light at Pha Chana Dai → down from the cliff → two-colour river, Khong Chiam → back to Ubon city

items.activity: Wake up, grab a few light things and walk from the camping ground to the cliff-edge viewpoint. Find a good spot and wait for first light.
items.note: The morning air is sharply cold, so bring a warm layer and a flashlight for the walk in the dark · the cliff edge is slippery, so watch your step near the drop

items.activity: Catch the sun coming up over the Mekong and the Lao mountains — the spot where sunlight first reaches Thailand. Take photos, sip the coffee you brewed yourself and soak it all in.
items.note: The actual sunrise time shifts with the season, roughly 05:30–06:15 · you need a clear sky to see it well; in the rainy season heavy cloud can block it

items.activity: Head back to the camping ground, eat the breakfast you packed, pack up the tent and trash, and get ready for the morning run down (07:30–09:30).
items.note: Carry every piece of trash back down · check you've got everything before boarding the run down — don't leave anything on the cliff

items.activity: Arrive at the Dong Na Tham checkpoint, pick up your car and drive down toward Khong Chiam town. Stop to freshen up and change into something comfortable.
items.note: The road down has curves, so take them carefully · if the early start has worn you out, pull over for some water before driving on

items.activity: Go to the two-colour river viewpoint in Khong Chiam, where the indigo Mun River meets the chalky, muddy Mekong. You can clearly see the line between the two colours on a clear day.
items.note: The two colours are sharpest in the dry season (Mar–May) · in the rainy season both run muddy and the dividing line fades · you can take a boat out for a closer look, price as agreed with the boat owner

items.activity: Have lunch by the Mekong in Khong Chiam, then sip a coffee with a river view at one of the riverside cafés before heading off, to shake off the early-morning tiredness.
items.note: A riverside café like Mong Khong Cafe & Camping has drinks from around 60 THB and a panoramic river view

items.activity: Drive back to Ubon city; you can stop for souvenirs along the way. You'll reach town around 3 p.m., leaving time to return a rental car or get to the airport.
items.note: If you've still got the energy and time, stop at Saeng Chan Waterfall (the waterfall that drops through a hole), in the same park area — it's at its best from the rainy season through early cool season

blocks.text: Which season to go, and when it's closed

blocks.html: Pha Chana Dai only opens in the cool and hot seasons; it closes in the rainy season because the way into the Dong Na Tham forest gets slippery and dangerous. The most popular window is the late-rains, early-cool season through winter, roughly November to February — cool, comfortable weather, clear skies, and a real shot at a sea of mist over the Mekong in the morning. The hot season still works, but the days get scorching and the mist thins out. Every time before you go, check with the Pha Taem National Park page that it's open and what the shuttle times are, since they adjust with the weather.

blocks.text: Getting there and what to pack

items: Your own vehicle is easiest — Ubon city to the Dong Na Tham checkpoint is about 100 km, and public transport barely reaches it. If you fly into Ubon airport and rent a car to drive yourself, that's the smoothest option.

Up the cliff means switching to a local vehicle — cars can't make it; park at the Dong Na Tham checkpoint and switch to a park/tour vehicle, on fixed up-and-down shuttle times, with the fare worked out on the spot by number of people.
Tent and bedding — the park rents them, but during busy periods they may run out, so bringing your own tent is the safer bet. The camping fee is 30 THB per person.
Flashlight, power bank, warm layer — there's no electricity on the cliff, and the wind is strong and cold at night, so even in the hot season you'll want a windbreaker.
Food and water for every meal — there are no shops on the cliff, so pack enough dinner, breakfast, water and snacks, and carry every piece of trash back down.
Sneakers — Pha Taem, Sao Chaliang and the paths on Pha Chana Dai are all stone and steps, and sandals slip easily.

blocks.text: What to eat before heading up and on the way down

blocks.html: Since you eat what you pack up on the cliff, the proper meals land in Khong Chiam both before you go up and on the way down. The standout here is fresh Mekong fish — giant catfish, Teepho catfish and river prawns — done as tom yum, grilled whole, or as larb, eaten with sticky rice and jaew dipping sauce. For the café crowd, there are river-view spots to rest up and shake off the tiredness.

items.name: Riverside restaurant, Khong Chiam
items.blurb: A local eatery on the riverbank, leaning on Mekong fish and river prawns, with a water's-edge setting. Good for a filling lunch before heading up the cliff.

items.name: Mong Khong Cafe & Camping
items.blurb: A café right on the Mekong with drinks, desserts, Thai–Isan–Western food and a camping zone. Drinks from around 60 THB, with a panoramic river view.

items.name: Khwam Song Jam Cafe
items.blurb: A chilled-out riverside café with house-roasted coffee, well-priced cakes and a savoury menu. You can sit and watch the river for ages — a good last cup before heading home.

blocks.title: The honest bit
blocks.html: Pha Chana Dai really is beautiful, but it really is rough too. You have to camp, there's no electricity, you carry your own gear up, and if the sky clouds over you might not get the first light you were hoping for. If your family has small kids or older relatives who struggle to walk, weigh it up first. Anyone who's fine with camping will find it well worth it — but if you'd rather take it easy, you might choose to watch the sunrise from the Pha Taem viewpoint instead, which you can drive right up to and is easier to reach.

faq.q: When is Pha Chana Dai open, and which season is best to visit?
faq.a: It reopened on 1 June 2025, but only opens in the cool and hot seasons; it closes in the rainy season because the way into the Dong Na Tham forest gets slippery and dangerous. The best window is the late-rains, early-cool season through winter, roughly November to February — cool weather, clear skies and a chance at a sea of mist. Always check with the Pha Taem National Park page that it's open before you go.

faq.q: Do you have to stay overnight at Pha Chana Dai, or can you go in the morning and come back?
faq.a: You can do it without staying over, by taking the morning run at 04:30–06:30 from the Dong Na Tham checkpoint — but that means getting up in the middle of the night from your lodging in Khong Chiam to make the shuttle, which is tight on time. The easier way, and the one that gets you more of the atmosphere, is to camp on the cliff for a night and stroll out to the viewpoint for first light.

faq.q: Can you drive up Pha Chana Dai in your own car?
faq.a: No. Cars can't reach the viewpoint. You have to park your car at the Dong Na Tham checkpoint and switch to a local vehicle or the park's tour vehicle for the rest of the way, on fixed up-and-down shuttle times. The fare is paid on the spot, charged by number of people or vehicle.

faq.q: How much are the entrance and camping fees at Pha Chana Dai?
faq.a: Park entry is 40 THB for Thai adults and 20 THB for children, 400 THB for foreign adults and 200 THB for children. The camping fee is 30 THB per person. If you don't have a tent, the park rents them for around 225 THB each with a sleeping mat and pillow. There's no electricity and no shops on the cliff, so bring your own food and a flashlight.

faq.q: Can you combine Pha Chana Dai with Pha Taem in one trip?
faq.a: Yes, and it fits really well, because both are within Pha Taem National Park. On day one you take in Pha Taem and Sao Chaliang and eat in Khong Chiam, then head up in the afternoon to camp on Pha Chana Dai. On the morning of day two you catch first light, then come down for the two-colour river before heading home. It works out to a neat 2 days, 1 night.
